headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible; Langflow’s unsandboxed server-side code raises the blast radius.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Langflow can read/write server files and chain agents in graph flows, while xonsh reads filesystem content and executes shell/Python expressions. A shared workspace or copied file content can therefore carry attacker-controlled instructions from agent_a into agent_b, though no direct shared channel is documented by default.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into a shared file that agent_b later reads as instructions
IF the deployment bridges outputs via a shared workspace or manual copy-paste
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic ingestion of file contents as prompts
Add provenance tags to files passed between agents
Require human review before agent_b executes agent_a outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch filesystem contents and have broad network egress. Langflow also stores per-flow credentials and uploaded files, while xonsh can expose environment variables and notebooks. In a shared workspace, either agent can surface sensitive data into the other’s outputs or outbound requests.
conditions: IF sensitive files or secrets are present in the shared workspace
IF either agent forwards file contents to external model providers or HTTP services
mitigations: Use separate credentials and workspaces
Redact secrets before either agent reads files
Restrict outbound domains for both agents
Mount sensitive directories read-only or not at all

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, read and write the filesystem, and use broad network egress. Langflow additionally runs unsandboxed Python server-side by default, so concurrent writes or side effects can collide with xonsh’s shell-driven mutations. No locking mechanism is documented, so conflict risk is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same writable directory
IF either agent mutates shared state without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize write operations with a lock file
Disable Langflow server-side code for shared runs
Run each agent in separate containers

D_cascading_error.rationale: Langflow’s graph-based flows can chain multiple agents, and xonsh can execute shell commands and Python expressions. If agent_b consumes agent_a’s outputs without verification, agent_a’s mistaken facts or malformed commands can cascade into real actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, so the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative input
IF agent_a output is routed into shell commands or API calls without validation
mitigations: Insert a validation step between agents
Require schema checks on all handoffs
Block direct shell interpolation of agent_a output
Log and review high-impact actions before execution

E_compliance.rationale: Langflow handles per-flow credentials and uploaded files on the server filesystem, while xonsh touches environment variables, notebooks, and filesystem contents. If regulated data is routed through both, differing retention or residency controls can be violated. No specific certifications or residency guarantees are documented for either agent, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF regulated data such as EU PII, PHI, or secrets is processed by both agents
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Align retention settings across both deployments
Document residency and deletion handling for each agent
